notes.title: Start here: LedgerFlow Lending and its derived stage
notes.body:
LedgerFlow Lending is a loan-origination workflow in Next.js, Prisma and PostgreSQL. An application moves through intake, verification, credit decisioning, conditions, approval, disbursement and the hand-off to servicing. No command ever sets the stage directly: after every write, a pure function recomputes it from the application's facts.

Read in this order:

1. `README.md`, including the security posture section (the login is a demo role switcher).
2. `docs/learning/guided-reading-path.md`: twelve stops through the code, each ending with a **Check**.
3. `docs/learning/concepts-demonstrated.md`: one concept per section, with where it falls short.
4. `docs/architecture/auth-and-permissions.md` and `request-lifecycle.md` when you want more detail.

Try each **Check** yourself before reading its answer line. The two files you will keep open are `src/services/workflow-reconciliation-service.ts` and `src/services/application-command-service.ts`.

excerpts.quote: The current stage is never set directly by a command.

readMore.why: Concepts, with where this code falls short.

notes.title: Concept: a stage computed from facts
notes.body:
Instead of a status column that commands overwrite, this app stores **facts** (intake completed, each verification's result, the decision, each condition, disbursement and hand-off times) and derives the stage from them. That keeps the stage consistent with the data, but it moves all of the policy into one function, and in that function the **order of the rules is the policy**.

Open `reconcileWorkflow` and write its rules down as a numbered list: the condition each one tests and the stage it returns. Then make yourself a few snapshots on paper (a funded loan with a late decision, an approved file with a problem condition, an approved file whose check result changes) and walk each through your list.

Next read `reconcileAndPersistStage` in the command service. Note exactly which comparison decides whether a row update and an `ApplicationTransition` are written. Finally, for `recordDecision` and `disburseApplication`, note which checks run before the transaction opens and what each refuses.

excerpts.quote: Stage is a function of facts.

readMore.why: The pure reconciler: read every rule in order.

notes.title: Concept: who may call what, and what they can see
notes.body:
Three separate mechanisms decide what a request can do.

**The route wrapper.** `createRouteHandler` in `src/lib/http/route-handler.ts` resolves the session, applies the permission the route declares, runs the handler and maps errors to statuses. List the permission each route under `src/app/api/` declares, then compare it with the role table in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts`. Look for role checks written inside the service too, and ask which one runs first.

**Record visibility.** `buildApplicationVisibilityWhere` in the repository restricts what some roles can read. Note the rule for each role, and where a party's `userId` comes from when an application is created.

**Provider events.** `ingestExternalVerificationEvent` takes simulated provider results. Find the two comparisons on `providerSequence` and note which operator each uses, what is stored in each case, and which actor id is passed on to the transition.

Finally note which kinds of error become 400, which keep their own status, and which become 500.

excerpts.quote: Each route declares one permission in its options object.

readMore.why: Session, permission and error handling for every route.
The visibility predicate and query shapes.

notes.title: Why a failed condition beats an approval
notes.body:
With intake done and every required verification PASSED, the verification rule does not fire. The decisioning rule fires only for PENDING or REFER, so an APPROVED decision passes it. The next rule looks for any condition whose status is FAILED and returns CONDITIONS with a reason naming that condition. The APPROVED rule comes later and is never reached.

- *APPROVED* would need the APPROVED rule to come before the condition rules.
- *CREDIT_DECISIONING* is returned only for PENDING or REFER decisions.
- *VERIFICATION* is wrong: that rule looks at verifications, not conditions.

notes.title: Why a late failed check pulls an approved file back
notes.body:
The newer event is applied, so EMPLOYMENT_CHECK is now FAILED. On reconcile, the verification rule sits above every decision rule: it fires when any verification has FAILED, or a required type is missing or not PASSED. It returns VERIFICATION with a reason naming the failed type, whatever the recorded decision says.

- *APPROVED stays* is wrong: the decision is a fact, but the stage is derived, and the verification rule wins.
- *CONDITIONS* is for failed or open closing conditions, not verifications.
- *DENIED* needs a DECLINED decision or `deniedAt`; a failed check alone does not decline.

notes.title: Why a funded loan can still end up DENIED
notes.body:
`recordDecision` refuses only when the derived stage is VERIFICATION, which a funded loan is not, so the decline is saved. The reconciler's first rule checks for a DECLINED decision or `deniedAt` before the rules for hand-off and disbursement. The application therefore becomes DENIED even though `disbursedAt` is set. The guided reading path calls this out: moving the DENIED rule below the funding rules would change the policy.

- *DISBURSEMENT* would need the funding rule first.
- *400* is wrong: nothing in the decision guard looks at disbursement.
- *SERVICING_HANDOFF* needs `servicingHandedOffAt`, which is not set.

notes.title: What happens to an out-of-order provider event
notes.body:
The command compares the incoming `providerSequence` with the verification's stored one. 3 is below 5, so `isOutOfOrder` is true and `shouldApply` is false. The event row is still written, with `appliedToWorkflow: false` and `receivedOutOfOrder: true`, so history keeps it, but the verification itself is not updated and stays PASSED.

- *Becomes FAILED* is the bug the guard exists to stop.
- *Refused with 409* is wrong: nothing throws; the event is stored.
- *Dropped without a row* is wrong: `createExternalEvent` runs for every event.

excerpts.quote: const isOutOfOrder = input.providerSequence < verification.providerSequence; const shouldApply = input.providerSequence >= verification.providerSequence;

notes.title: Why an equal sequence number is applied again
notes.body:
The apply test is `>=`, so an event whose sequence equals the stored one counts as fresh. The FAILED result overwrites PASSED. The out-of-order flag uses `<`, so the event is not marked out of order either. The concepts doc lists this among the guard's weaknesses: a provider that re-sends or reorders events with the same sequence can flip a result.

- *Ignored as already seen* would need `>` instead of `>=`.
- *Stored as out of order* would need the `<` test to be true, and 5 is not below 5.
- *Refused by a unique index* is wrong: events have no unique key on sequence.

notes.title: Why the route refuses a loan officer before the service is asked
notes.body:
The submit route declares `permission: "application:submit"`. `createRouteHandler` asserts that permission before calling the handler, and in the role table only BORROWER has it. A LOAN_OFFICER therefore gets **403** from the wrapper. The service's own check, which would let borrowers and loan officers through, never runs. The concepts doc notes that this inner check contradicts the matrix.

- *200* would be true only if the wrapper did not check permissions.
- *403 from the service* is wrong: the service is never reached, and it does not check the creator.
- *400 for confirmReady* is wrong: the body schema requires `true`, and the request fails before it is parsed.

notes.title: Why a decision is refused while a check is pending
notes.body:
`recordDecision` derives the current stage from the stored facts before it writes anything. With DOCUMENT_CHECK still PENDING, a required verification is not PASSED, so the derived stage is VERIFICATION, and the command throws `badRequest`, a **400** with the message about verification checks. No transaction is opened.

- *200, stage unchanged* is wrong: the guard throws before saving.
- *409* is wrong: the helper used is `badRequest`.
- *403* is wrong: underwriters hold `application:record-decision`; the refusal is about state, not role.

excerpts.quote: throw badRequest("All required verification checks must pass before decisioning.");

notes.title: Why a reason-only change still writes a transition
notes.body:
`reconcileAndPersistStage` writes when the derived stage differs from the stored one **or** the derived reason differs from `stageReason`. If only the reason changed, it still updates the row (bumping `stateVersion`) and creates an `ApplicationTransition` whose `fromStage` equals its `toStage`. The decision flow triggers this, because `recordDecision` overwrites `stageReason` with the underwriter's text and the reconciler then puts its own reason back.

- *Nothing* would need the stage comparison alone.
- *Reason only, no transition* is wrong: both writes are in the same branch.
- *Throws* is wrong: nothing forbids equal stages in a transition.

notes.title: Why a servicing agent gets 404 on a pre-funding file
notes.body:
Neither read route declares a permission, so the repository's visibility filter is the only gate. For SERVICING_AGENT it limits results to the DISBURSEMENT and SERVICING_HANDOFF stages. A file in CONDITIONS does not match, the lookup returns nothing, and the service throws `notFound`: **404** "Application not found."

- *200, no permission needed* is half right: no permission is declared, but the visibility filter still applies.
- *403* is wrong: the code reports a missing record, not a refused one.
- *200 with data hidden* is wrong: the record is not returned at all.

notes.title: How one borrower can give another access
notes.body:
For borrowers, visibility is "some party on this application has my user id". The create schema lets each party carry an optional `userId`, and nothing checks that it belongs to the caller. Borrower A can therefore set the co-applicant's `userId` to B's id, and B now sees the application. User ids are easy to find, because `GET /api/session` lists the demo users.

- *Only the creator can read* is wrong: the rule is party membership, not authorship.
- *After a loan officer approves the link* is wrong: there is no such step.
- *Checked against the caller* is wrong: the schema accepts any non-empty string.

notes.title: Why a huge requested amount is a 500
notes.body:
The create schema only requires `requestedAmount` to be positive. One trillion passes validation and reaches the insert, where the `Decimal(12,2)` column (at most ten digits before the point) overflows and PostgreSQL rejects the value. Prisma raises an error that is neither a `ZodError` nor an `AppError`, so `errorResponse` logs it and returns **500** "Internal server error."

- *400 out of range* would need a `.max()` on the schema.
- *Capped* and *stored as a float* are wrong: the database refuses the value instead of changing it.

notes.title: Who a provider-driven transition is credited to
notes.body:
After storing the event, the command calls `reconcileAndPersistStage` with an actor id of `null` when the event was applied, and the user's id when it was not. `createTransition` sets `triggeredBySystem` to `actorUserId === null`. An applied event that changes the stage therefore produces a transition with no user and `triggeredBySystem: true`. The audit log row for the same event still names the loan officer.

- *The loan officer* is who the stale-event path and the audit log record, not the applied transition.
- *The provider reference* is stored on the verification, not used as an actor.
- *No transition* is wrong: a stage change always writes one.

notes.title: Concept: the browser half of every request
notes.body:
The server side of this app is carefully layered: route wrapper, zod schema, service, repository, presenter. The browser side has its own layers, and the later questions in this pack are about them and about how a change in one layer reaches the others.

Read `src/components/providers/query-provider.tsx` first and note the client's default options. Then open every file in `src/hooks/`. Make two lists: each `queryKey` a query defines, and each key a mutation invalidates when it succeeds. Next to each query, write which page mounts it. Then read `src/lib/api/fetcher.ts` line by line and note the order of its steps.

In `src/components/applications/application-detail-client.tsx`, list the `can...` flags that enable each button and set them beside the role table in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts`. Finally, follow one field from `prisma/schema.prisma` through `src/lib/validation/application-schemas.ts`, the service's input type and the hook types, and mark each type as generated, inferred or written by hand.

excerpts.quote: function useWorkflowMutation( applicationId: string, path: string, method = "POST", ) {

readMore.why: The session query and the role-switch mutation.
The one function every hook calls to reach the API.

notes.title: Why a role switch leaves the old detail on screen
notes.body:
The switch's `onSuccess` invalidates two keys, `["session"]` and `["applications"]`. React Query compares a filter key with each cached key element by element from the front, so `["applications"]` matches the list and nothing else: the detail lives under `["application", id]`, whose first element is a different string. The detail query is not refetched and not even marked stale. Nothing else asks for it again, so the page keeps rendering the data fetched with the officer's cookie, while the buttons recompute from the new role.

- *A not-found state* would need the detail to refetch under the borrower's cookie.
- *An empty page* would need the cache cleared; a new cookie does not touch it.
- *The borrower's view* is what a correct invalidation (or `queryClient.clear()` on login) would produce.

notes.title: The page's button rules are a drifted copy of the role table
notes.body:
The detail page decides which buttons to enable from its own flags, and `canManageVerifications` lets UNDERWRITER in. The server decides from the role table, where only LOAN_OFFICER holds `application:manage-verifications`. The verifications route declares that permission, and `createRouteHandler` asserts it before the handler runs, so the underwriter's click comes back **403** without the service ever being called.

The lesson is about where authority lives. UI gating is a convenience; the route's declared permission is the rule. Two hand-maintained copies of one matrix drift, which is why the build journal lists this mismatch.

- *201* would need UNDERWRITER in the role table, not just in the page's flag.
- *404* would come from the visibility lookup, which never runs after the 403.
- *400* would come from the body schema, which is parsed inside the handler, after the permission check.

readMore.why: The role table the server actually enforces.

notes.title: Invalidation refetches what is on screen, and only that
notes.body:
The workflow hook throws the POST's response away: its `onSuccess` only invalidates the detail key and the list key. By default `invalidateQueries` marks every matching query stale but refetches only the **active** ones, those with a mounted observer. On the detail page that is the detail query, so the browser sends one GET for it. The list's observer unmounted with the dashboard, so the list is just flagged and refetches when the dashboard mounts again.

The decision route had already returned the full detail, so a `setQueryData` with the response would have saved that GET.

- *Two GETs* would need the list query to be mounted on the detail page.
- *None* describes `setQueryData`, which no hook calls.
- *One for the list* reverses which query is active; the detail page never reads the list.

excerpts.quote: onSuccess: async () => { await Promise.all([ queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["application", applicationId] }),

readMore.why: The repo's own review of the React Query boundary.

notes.title: A detail page with no error state shows loading forever
notes.body:
The App Router page is a server component that only awaits `params` and renders the client component; it loads no data and checks no session. All data comes from the client query. When the API answers 404, `apiFetch` throws, the query ends in its error state, and its data stays undefined because it never succeeded. The component has one branch for that case, the Loading block, and no component in `src/` reads a query error. So the borrower sees Loading application... indefinitely.

- *A not-found message* would need the component to read `detailQuery.error`.
- *A redirect* would need the server page to fetch or check access, and it does neither.
- *Hidden parties* would need the presenter to run, but the service refuses before presenting.

notes.title: An 8,999-value id space under a unique index
notes.body:
Public ids are `APP-` plus `randomInt(1000, 9999)`, and `randomInt` excludes its upper bound, so there are 8,999 possible ids. The column is unique. Once about half the space is used, a random draw lands on a taken id about half the time; even at 112 rows the chance that some pair has collided is already near 50%. The insert then fails with Prisma's unique-constraint error, which the wrapper does not recognise, so it logs it and answers 500. The transaction rolls back, so no half-created file or audit row is left.

- *A retry* would need a loop around the insert; there is none.
- *409* would need the wrapper to map Prisma's P2002; it maps only ZodError and AppError.
- *A suffix* would need id generation that checks the table first.

notes.title: A retried create is a second create
notes.body:
The create flow has no way to recognise a retry. The form disables its button only while the mutation is pending and never clears its fields, so after a dropped response the same values can be sent again. The schema carries no request id, and the service always inserts a new application with a newly drawn public id, its parties and an audit row. The only unique columns on an application are its id and public id, so the database has nothing to refuse either. The result is two files.

The usual fix is an idempotency key: the client generates it once per form, sends it with every attempt, and the server stores it under a unique index and returns the first result on a repeat.

- No step matches on parties, no key is sent, and no index covers purpose or amount.

readMore.why: The create transaction: application, parties and audit row.

notes.title: Three copies of one input type, and only one of them checked
notes.body:
The create payload is described three times: the zod schema (whose inferred type the route gets from `parse`), the service's hand-written `input` type, and the client's `CreateApplicationInput`. Adding a required field to the schema changes only the first. Passing the wider parsed object to the service's narrower parameter is legal TypeScript, because excess-property checks apply to object literals only, and the form is typed by its own copy, so `tsc` reports nothing. At runtime the form's body lacks the field, `parse` throws, and every create gets a 400.

Deriving the other two from the schema with `z.infer` would turn this into a compile error in the form.

- *tsc fails in the form*: the form never imports the schema.
- *tsc fails in the service*: a wider argument is allowed.
- *Stored as null*: parse rejects first, and there is no column.

readMore.why: The client's own copy of the create payload type.

notes.title: Generated types flow to the server, not to the browser
notes.body:
The create schema validates `productType` with `z.enum(LoanProductType)`, and `LoanProductType` is imported from the generated Prisma client. Regenerating after adding JUMBO therefore widens server validation with no further edit, and the pushed schema lets the insert store it. The browser does not import `@prisma/client`: its payload type spells out four products and the select renders four hard-coded options. So the API accepts JUMBO while the form can never send it, and nothing fails to compile.

This is the mirror image of the previous ripple: generated types keep the server honest automatically, while hand-written client copies go quietly out of date.

- *The form* is not built from the enum.
- *Neither* ignores the import on the schema line.
- *Both* assumes client code imports Prisma's types; it does not.

notes.title: The cookie names the user, the database names the role
notes.body:
The session cookie holds only the user id and an HMAC of that id. On every request the route wrapper resolves the session again: it checks the signature, loads the user row by id and builds the session from that row, role included. A role edited in the database therefore applies to the very next API call, with the new permissions and the new visibility filter.

That is the trade against a token that embeds claims: one primary-key lookup per request buys instant role changes and revocation by deleting the user.

- *At the next login* would be true of a token that carries the role.
- *Never* misreads the signature, which covers the id alone.
- *The browser's session query* changes what the UI displays, not what the server enforces.

notes.title: Parse first, check status second loses the status
notes.body:
`apiFetch` calls `response.json()` before it looks at `response.ok`. The app's own routes always answer JSON, so this works for every error they produce. A proxy's HTML 502 page is not JSON: `json()` rejects with a SyntaxError, the function exits there, and the `ApiClientError` that would carry the status is never built. The hook's error is a parse error with no status, so a caller cannot tell a gateway failure from a broken response.

Checking `ok` and the content type before parsing, and falling back to the status text, keeps the 502.

- *ApiClientError with 502* is what the code would produce if it checked `ok` first.
- *The HTML as the message* would need a text fallback; there is none.
- *No error* would need a catch around `json()`.

excerpts.quote: const payload = (await response.json()) as { error?: string };

notes.title: An upsert's update branch decides what a repeat request changes
notes.body:
The command hands PENDING and sequence 0 to the repository, but the repository writes them through an upsert keyed on the (application, type) unique index. Those values are used only when no row exists. When CREDIT_PULL already exists, the update branch runs, and it sets `providerReference` and `startedAt` and nothing else. The verification stays PASSED at sequence 5 with the new reference. The command still writes its audit row and re-runs the reconcile, which finds nothing new.

That makes the request safe to repeat, but it also means re-requesting a check cannot restart it; only a provider event with a high enough sequence can change its status.

- *PENDING at 0* is the create branch, which does not run.
- *Two rows* are ruled out by the unique index.
- *409* would need a refusal; the upsert simply updates.
